st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: The advisory accepts that Gen AI will reshape law-firm production economics and gradually push pricing toward a hybrid mix rather than immediately eliminate hourly billing. It materially extends the cluster by quantifying current investment and billing expectations and arguing that the cost of AI adoption will increase the need for scale and drive consolidation.
qs: While some will achieve this growth organically, we believe that the need to fund Gen AI investments will place pressure on the expense base of law firms and drive further industry consolidation.
We can expect to see more fixed fees, subscription services and value-based billing – and more of a mix of fee structures based on the type of work done.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The advisory accepts the cluster’s core work-redesign thesis and materially extends it with large-firm survey evidence and forecasts: repetitive work shifts to Gen AI, strategic and judgment-intensive work moves toward senior lawyers, junior roles contract, and demand grows for technology, data and knowledge-management specialists. It also develops the operating-model implications through expected infrastructure investment and pricing change, although it offers little direct evidence on jagged task capability, user expertise or verification.

st.t: Firm profitability: Revenue growth can hide cost fragility
st.an: The advisory directly supports the proposition that strong revenue growth does not by itself demonstrate durable profitability. It attributes 11.3% revenue growth largely to collections, rates and modest demand growth, while documenting hiring-led expense growth, declining productivity, slower collections and widespread realization erosion. Its strong full-year forecast is a near-term outlook, not a rejection of those cost and collection vulnerabilities.

st.t: Law-firm pyramid: Efficiency threatens revenue and training
st.an: The advisory supports the cluster’s expectation that Gen AI will reduce reliance on junior production and reshape leverage toward experienced lawyers and AI-support professionals. Its evidence is survey-based and predictive, so it reinforces anticipated staffing change without establishing realised employment contraction or addressing the training and revenue consequences in depth.

Meanwhile, we can expect to see more investment in professionals supporting Gen AI, including data scientists, as well as technology and knowledge management professionals.

st.t: Partnership structure: AI tests governance beyond capital scarcity
st.an: The advisory supports the synthesis’s qualified view that capital scarcity alone does not explain adaptation: it describes firms as better capitalized while anticipating greater investment needs. It also supports aligning partner capital with strategy and recognizes outside-investment structures without claiming that they resolve broader governance or regulatory constraints.

kp.k: Survey findings and leadership expectations underpin the outlook
kp.d: The advisory combines financial survey data and conversations with law firm leaders. Its sources comprise the Citi Annual Survey Database of 195 US- and UK-headquartered firms, the Citi 9mo’25 Flash Survey of 185 firms, and the Citi Law Firm Leaders Survey of 55 large firms headquartered in the US, UK, China and India. Observed financial results should be distinguished from leaders’ expectations and the authors’ predictions about Gen AI through 2027 and 2035.
qs: as well as conversations with law firm leaders.
Percentages used in the Figures may not add exactly to 100% due to rounding.

kp.k: Strong revenue growth accompanies rising staffing and technology costs
kp.d: For the first nine months of 2025, the advisory reports revenue growth of 11.3%, demand growth of 1.9%, and rate increases of 9.6%. Headcount rose 2.9%, equity partner headcount declined 0.5%, leverage increased 4.3%, and income partner headcount increased 6%. Headcount investment outpaced demand, with productivity declining 0.6%. Expenses increased 9.1%, reflecting salaried lawyer growth, a more senior staffing mix, technology investment and professional staff upskilling; the report does not attribute these aggregate changes solely to AI.

kp.k: Lawyer leverage was already becoming more senior
kp.d: During 2019–24, large firms increased lawyer leverage at an average annual rate of 2.7%, reaching 4.57 salaried lawyers per equity partner in 2024. The mix shifted toward counsel and income partners and away from associates and temporary or other lawyers. This is historical evidence of a more senior, expensive staffing model, rather than proof of AI-driven restructuring. Looking ahead, 67% of large firms expect to increase lawyer leverage through 2027, and 72% plan more income partners.

kp.k: Associate growth plans favor seniority over entry-level expansion
kp.d: Although 86% of large firms plan to expand overall associate ranks through 2027, only 35% plan larger first-year classes and 37% larger summer classes. The authors interpret this gap as suggesting a more senior associate demographic, likely driven by Gen AI adoption, while explicitly questioning the future supply of experienced associates. Figure 8 labels 2025 class sizes as projected: average first-year classes of 109 versus 120 in 2024, and summer classes of 134 versus 122.
qs: only 35% plan to increase the size of their first-year associate classes.
Similarly, only 37% of large firms plan to increase the size of their summer associate classes through 2027.
This begs the question: ‘How will firms have enough senior associates in the longer term if they have trained fewer first year associates?’

kp.k: AI is expected to reshape, not necessarily reduce, leverage
kp.d: In the 2025 leaders survey, 25% of large firms expect Gen AI-related lawyer leverage changes by 2027, compared with 9% expecting near-term changes in the prior survey. By 2035, 63% expect changes, compared with 43% looking to 2034 in the prior survey. The authors predict a transition from pyramid to cylinder, with fewer juniors and more senior strategic work as AI replaces repetitive, low-value tasks. These are expectations, not measured displacement outcomes, and do not necessarily imply lower leverage.

kp.k: Professional staffing faces junior reductions and specialist investment
kp.d: Within two years, 36% of large firms expect Gen AI to affect professional staffing models, almost double the proportion anticipating near-term change in the previous survey. By 2035, more than two thirds expect changes. The authors anticipate reductions or elimination of junior roles alongside investment in data scientists, technology professionals and knowledge management professionals. These forecasts concern professional staff separately from lawyer leverage.
qs: Within the next two years, 36% of large firms expect Gen AI to affect their professional staffing models, almost double the proportion of firms who expected near-term change in last year’s survey.
And by 2035, more than two thirds of large firms expect to make changes – most likely the reduction or elimination of junior roles.
Meanwhile, we can expect to see more investment in professionals supporting Gen AI, including data scientists, as well as technology and knowledge management professionals.

kp.k: Fewer support staff have not meant lower staffing costs
kp.d: During 2019–24, large firms reduced professional staff per lawyer from 0.89 to 0.8 and secretaries per lawyer from 0.22 to 0.16. Nevertheless, professional staff salary costs per lawyer increased by $20,000 to $134,000, including a $9,000 increase in 2024 alone. The authors connect this pressure to more expensive specialist roles. Through 2027, 71% of firms project growth in technology staff excluding data scientists, and 71% project growth in data scientists; only 30% expect overall professional staff leverage growth.

kp.k: Income partner expansion poses profitability and promotion challenges
kp.d: Income partner numbers grew an average 6.4% annually during 2019–24, compared with 0.7% for equity partners. For 2020–24 additions, firms reported above-break-even success for 66% of promoted and 56% of lateral income partners. In the advisory’s 2024 contribution analysis, income partners contributed $351,000 per lawyer, versus $696,000 for counsel and $552,000 for associates. The authors acknowledge retention and client-facing benefits of the partner title but warn that expansion could create a backlog of lawyers expecting equity promotion. This qualifies the economics of the anticipated senior staffing shift.
qs: However, the overall income partner success rate is much lower for both promoted (66% above break-even) and lateral income partners (56% above break-even).
Talent retention is a major driver of the decision by a number of firms to introduce the income partner title.
This will force firms to make some hard decisions on who to promote and who to move out.

kp.k: AI investment is small but universally expected to grow
kp.d: Gen AI became large firms’ leading technology priority, ahead of cloud computing and cybersecurity. Actual Gen AI investment, including related staff and consulting, averaged 0.11% of 2024 revenue against 2.39% for total technology spending. All firms in the relevant large-firm sample expect increased Gen AI investment over the next two years. The advisory reports that many firms consider this necessary to remain competitive, while cost recovery remains unresolved; fewer write-offs are presented as a prospective efficiency benefit.
qs: accounted for 0.11% of 2024 revenue, according to Citi data, compared with 2.39% total technology spend.
Unsurprisingly, 100% of that large firm sample expect to increase their investment in Gen AI over the next two years.
The big question is how firms will recover the likely significant cost of this investment.
many firms believe that this is a necessary and unavoidable investment, required to stay relevant in the industry.

kp.k: AI could accelerate alternatives to hourly billing
kp.d: The leaders survey finds that 35% of large firms expect Gen AI-related changes to billable-hour models by 2027 and 69% by 2035. Near-term uncertainty remains substantial: 24% expect no change and 41% do not know. The authors anticipate more fixed fees, subscriptions, value-based billing and work-specific combinations of fee structures, rather than reporting an already completed transition.
qs: Within two years, 35% of large firms expect to make changes to their billable hour models as a result of Gen AI, as illustrated in Figure 22.
That said, the majority don’t know if they will make changes or don’t plan to.
We can expect to see more fixed fees, subscription services and value-based billing – and more of a mix of fee structures based on the type of work done.

kp.k: Alternative fees grow amid existing realization pressure
kp.d: Separate from AI-specific forecasts, AFA revenue increased from 19.9% in 2019 to 23.5% in 2024, with 23.6% expected for 2025; the report includes fixed, capped and blended-rate fees in this category. Pre-negotiated discounts accounted for 46.5% of revenue in 2024 and were projected at the same level in 2025. Through 2027, 74% of firms expect an increasing AFA revenue share. Accrual realization fell from 82.3% to 80.8% during 2019–24, with firms citing discount pressure, rate increases and write-offs. The report does not present AI as the demonstrated cause of these historical trends.
qs: any form of AFA (fixed, capped or blended rate fees)
This is a clear trend.

kp.k: AI costs could increase scale and consolidation pressures
kp.d: The authors argue that firms will need scale to absorb Gen AI investment, achieved organically or through consolidation. They also recommend reviewing three-to-five-year strategic plans and raising partner capital accordingly, because paid-in capital growth has not kept pace with net income while investment requirements are rising. This is a funding recommendation and market forecast, not evidence that AI has already caused particular mergers.
qs: In order to absorb this investment cost, we believe that firms will need scale.
While some will achieve this growth organically, we believe that the need to fund Gen AI investments will place pressure on the expense base of law firms and drive further industry consolidation.

kp.k: Outside investment may target smaller, high-volume legal businesses
kp.d: The authors expect continued interest in equity investment and private credit for law firms. They note that almost all US states prohibit non-lawyer equity ownership and report interest in managed services organizations as a means of enabling outside investment. They consider private equity investment less likely in large firms and more likely among smaller firms delivering repetitive, high-volume services that could benefit from technology funding. This is a prospective financing mechanism, not a report of regulatory liberalization or completed investments.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Citi and Hildebrandt predict more efficient legal work, more senior staffing, changes in pricing, increased investment costs and consolidation, and AI-related growth in some legal practices.
pts.d: The advisory, principally authored by Gretta Rusanow and Brad Hildebrandt, predicts that Gen AI will replace repetitive, low-value work and increase the importance of strategic advice requiring experience and human judgment. It anticipates a shift from pyramid-shaped lawyer staffing to a cylinder, rather than necessarily a reduction in the ratio of salaried lawyers to equity partners. It predicts fewer junior associates and a more senior associate population, raising a question about the future supply of trained senior associates. Professional staff changes are expected to include reductions or elimination of junior roles alongside investment in data scientists, technology professionals and knowledge management professionals. The authors expect efficiency to reduce write-offs but also expect AI investment costs to require greater scale and encourage consolidation. They foresee more fixed fees, subscriptions, value-based billing and work-specific combinations of fee structures. Separately, they predict growth in complex commercial and intellectual property litigation as Gen AI use grows, and identify AI data-center construction, alongside return to office, as a driver of real estate activity. The discussion of outside capital identifies smaller and repetitive, high-volume legal-service firms as potential beneficiaries of technology investment; this is a broader technology claim rather than a separately quantified AI prediction.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists of firm financial surveys, leaders’ reported expectations and the authors’ conversations and advisory experience; the AI outcomes are predominantly forecasts rather than measured effects.
pts.d: The source describes an annual survey database of 195 US- and UK-headquartered firms, a nine-month 2025 flash survey of 185 firms, and a leaders survey of 55 large firms headquartered in the US, UK, China and India. The AI expectations principally come from the July 2025 leaders survey. For lawyer leverage, 25% expect AI-related changes by 2027 and 63% by 2035, compared with 9% by 2026 and 43% by 2034 in the previous survey. For professional staffing, 36% expect changes within two years and more than two thirds by 2035. For billing, 35% expect AI-related changes by 2027 and 69% by 2035. Citi reports actual 2024 AI technology expenditure, including associated staff and consulting, of 0.11% of revenue versus 2.39% for total technology expenditure; all firms in the cited large-firm sample expect increased AI investment over the next two years. The authors infer a more senior associate mix from the gap between the 86% planning overall associate growth through 2027 and the 35% planning first-year class growth and 37% planning summer class growth. This is an interpretation of hiring intentions, not a measured causal effect of AI. Efficiency, replacement of repetitive tasks, consolidation and practice-demand predictions are supported by the authors’ interpretation and experience, not by task benchmarks or quantified AI productivity studies presented here.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The advisory distinguishes near-term changes through 2027 from broader transformation by 2035, while acknowledging uncertainty about implementation, cost recovery and long-run demand.
pts.d: The outlook is written in 2025 for 2026 and beyond. Its near-term AI survey horizon is 2027; the decade horizon is 2035. Comparisons with the prior survey refer to different endpoint years, 2026 and 2034. The authors do not predict universal immediate restructuring: only a minority expect near-term lawyer-leverage or billing-model changes, and many respondents remain uncertain. Nor do they equate a more senior staffing shape with necessarily lower leverage. Efficiency and fewer write-offs are anticipated benefits, while cost recovery remains unresolved; consolidation is predicted on the condition that firms need scale to absorb investment costs, with organic growth also possible. Litigation growth is linked to growing Gen AI use, and real estate growth partly to data-center construction. The conclusion explicitly leaves uncertain how AI changes to clients’ businesses will affect long-run legal demand. The source’s disclosure also states that its opinions are subject to change.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected population is large law firms and their lawyers and professional staff; smaller firms and corporate clients appear in the market-structure and demand discussion.
pts.d: Large firms are the population for the reported AI expectations, not the entire legal profession. Junior associates and junior professional staff face anticipated reductions in roles or relative hiring emphasis; senior lawyers are expected to undertake more strategic, judgment-intensive work. The senior-lawyer training pipeline may be affected if fewer first-year associates are developed. Data scientists, technology professionals and knowledge management professionals are expected to see increased investment. Firms and their partners must fund AI implementation and reconsider delivery, staffing and billing models. Larger firms may acquire smaller and mid-size firms as cost pressures increase the need for scale. Smaller firms and firms specializing in repetitive, high-volume services are discussed as possible recipients of outside capital supporting technology investment, although the source considers private equity investment in large firms less likely. Corporate clients may encounter changing fee structures and advisory needs, but the long-run demand implications of AI changes to their own businesses remain uncertain. Litigation and real estate practices may gain AI-related work. The advisory does not make a specific access-to-justice claim or quantify benefits for underserved individuals.
